why?
why game devs dont optimize their games from consoles to PC?

The Japanese hate PC gaming so they have a long history of not developing for PC at all. Recently games like Dark Souls have taken advantage of the fact that good games will sell on the PC platform and now more Asian publishers are putting their games on PC, but they still prefer development for PS4 and Nintendo, before PC and XBone.

Western game devs spend more time on consoles because the console kiddies will pay for anything regardless of quality. See any Ubisoft game, Evolve, and the CoD crowd.

Consoles are also for the most part not backwards compatible. PCs on the other hand can continue playing most of the games that have been developed for them for like at least the last 15 years. This means that their is much less choice on console so each AAA release is a big fish in a little pond whereas a new game on PC has to be better than an older comparable game on PC.

And lastly, the consoles have fixed the specs which makes game development much easier. PCs have much more variables which is harder to optimize for.

All (recent) games are developed on PCs.

Probably doesn't answer your question, but it adds context.

Most games that run like shit on PC also run like shit on consoles. Console gamers are just used to it - the low fps and low resolution with low graphics settings. The PC crowd is more likely to notice that a game runs like shit because we can change the graphics settings and we can have better hardware to test the limits. For example, GTA IV and Arkham Knight run like shit on PC, however if you play those games at the low settings and 720p then you will get the same 30 or less than 30 fps that the consoles get, with all the fps drops. Compare that to all the other games on consoles that run at 720p and 30 fps, there isn't much of a difference.

Sometimes you just can't without sinking a lot of time, money, and effort into rewriting a significant portion of the games code.

Virtually every piece of software that you'd use today is built on top of a series of other pieces of software called libraries. These libraries simplify how you write code because you can import the library and use prebuilt functions to save you a lot of time and effort, you don't have to understand how file input and output operations work you just need to use the read and write functions properly and everything is taken care of for you. The same is true with more complex operations like making a draw call to have a scene rendered,

Draw calls are essentially what the games logic tells the API ( DirectX & OpenGL/Vulkan are API's) what it wants to render and the API in combination with the graphics card driver doing all the heavy lifting required to make things happen. Now the API is effectively just a big external library that a game can use to interface with the graphics card drivers (which then interfaces with the graphics cards hardware) without having to write code specifically for that graphics card but the part where it gets tricky is when your API just does things inefficiently or worse your code is just inefficient but your API makes up for it by taking a shortcut or the costs of doing things inefficiently don't really matter because the game runs at an acceptable speed anyway.

This is where the really big disparity between whats possible on relatively weak console hardware but runs like shit on a PC comes from. A consoles API does not have the same kind of limitations or legacy issues that might bog down a modern PC. You can pass the same instructions into the same library of the "equivalent" API and or driver software on a desktop PC but that does not necessarily mean that it will be processed the same way, a consoles API might have a unique method of handling draw calls that optimizes how something is rendered where as on a desktop its API might not have this specific kind of optimization unless you specifically write it into your code to use parts of the API improperly (this is why a lot of big AAA games need day one driver fixes). The results are identical but the time taken to get there has increased to the point where performance has started to suffer.

When this starts to happen you look at how things are, you weigh up if spending money on optimization is best course of action or simply outline a higher minimum spec that you officially support. It will always be cheaper to raise the minimum and recommended specs then it is to pay a software engineer for the time it would take to ensure maximum performance.
